### [Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)

Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.

 Oct. 1, 2026 

**The impact**

Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.

**Dig deeper**

In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.

Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.

The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.

Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

**The basics**

Two California governors faced recall in the last 30 years. In 2021, Gavin Newsom survived an effort [to recall him amid the COVID-19 pandemic](https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-26/2021-california-recall-election-guide). But in 2003, [Gray Davis was ousted from office](https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html) and replaced by Arnold Schwarzenegger. Now, voters will consider significant changes to recall rules for state elected officials.

Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time. Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.

### [Your guide to Proposition 5: Big changes to recall elections in California](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-5-recall-changes-voter-guide)

Prop 5 would make major changes to how recall elections are conducted in California, especially affecting the office of governor.

 Oct. 1, 2026 

**The impact**

This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system. Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official. Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date. In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.

The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

**Dig deeper**

California’s rules for recalling politicians date to the [Progressive era](https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html) and were seen at the time as a way to give more power to voters.

But there have been concerns in recent years that the process needs reform, especially after the 2021 recall that Newsom overwhelmingly beat back; it cost local and state governments more than $200 million.

After the Newsom recall failed, the Legislature began a bipartisan task force to suggest changes.

The Trump administration has frozen, terminated or delayed billions in congressionally approved research grants since last year. Proposition 38 aims to backfill some of that loss by creating a stable source of money to fund immunology and immunotherapy research.

[Proposition 38](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide) would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research to uncover treatments that help the immune system fight diseases such as cancer or Alzheimer’s disease more efficiently.

### [Your guide to Proposition 38: Immunology and immunotherapy research funding](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide)

Prop 38 aims to fund immunotherapy research to prevent and cure diseases through bonds. An opponent says it is a debt-financed model that prioritizes a few diseases.

 Oct. 26, 2026 

**The impact**

The measure would require at least $4.2 billion of the funds to be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s. It also would authorize the state to enter a partnership with an immunology and immunotherapy research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health and allocate half of the bond revenue to it.

The remaining funds would be used for competitive grants that focus solely on immunology and immunotherapy research.

Californians would take on an increased cost of $500 million to $600 million annually to repay the bond for about 20 years, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.

The Yes on 38 campaign says the proposition pays for itself; 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the state to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest. However, it’s difficult to predict whether any research projects will lead to marketable treatments.

**Dig deeper**

Proposition 38 was backed by organizations including the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research and the ALS Assn. as well as a majority of local chapters of Democratic organizations across the state. Supporters say the proposed funding could give those afflicted with chronic illness hope and potentially more options for treatment.

Its opponents have said the proposed criteria for awarding the grant funding would appear to create an extremely small pool of qualified recipients. Only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, co-founded by billionaire Gary K. Michelson, would qualify under the proposed criteria, according to No on 38.

Robin Swanson, spokesperson for Yes on 38, said “lots of institutions would qualify for funds under this measure.” But she said at a virtual news conference in mid-September that it was “very likely” that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy “will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria.”

Ultimately, Swanson said, the decision lies with the California Department of Public Health.

### [Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)

Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.

**The impact**

The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.

**Dig deeper**

The California Taxpayers Assn., the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce and others back the proposition. They say it would result in the government spending taxpayer dollars more wisely while improving transparency.

The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the group behind the proposed billionaire tax, opposes Proposition 41. **The basics**

[Proposition 42](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide) would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.

Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.

### [Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)

Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.

 Oct. 1, 2026 

The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.

**Dig deeper**

The measure states that its purpose is to protect Californians’ ability to save for retirement and the future, though opponents say it’s meant to trick voters into canceling the billionaire tax.

“Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California — we need protection against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings,” supporters wrote in favor of the measure. The California Small Business Assn., California Senior Alliance, California Professional Firefighters and other groups back the measure.

“Don’t be fooled — Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes,” SEIU-UHW Chief of Staff Suzanne Jimenez wrote in arguments against the proposition. “It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes.”

**The basics**

[Proposition 44](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-44-health-clinic-spending-voter-guide) asks voters to require federally funded community health centers to spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on “program services advancing their charitable purpose.”

### [Your guide to Proposition 44: Federally funded health clinic spending](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-44-health-clinic-spending-voter-guide)

Prop 44 asks voters to require federally funded community health centers to spend at least 90% of their total annual revenue on “program services advancing their charitable purpose.”

 Oct. 1, 2026 

**The impact**

If the proposition passes, the state attorney general will be responsible for determining what services fall into that category. If spending on administrative or non-healthcare functions exceeded 10% of total revenue, a clinic would have to pay a penalty equal to the amount it overspent.

**Dig deeper**

Proposition 44 was backed by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the same union that is pushing Proposition 40, the controversial billionaire tax. The union appears to be the main supporter of the proposal and says the restrictions would prevent excessive spending on executive salaries, fundraisers and other administrative expenses.

There is a diverse array of opponents, including the California Medical Assn., the California Teachers Assn., the Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, the state Democratic Party and the state Chamber of Commerce. They say the proposition’s vague wording could result in vital services being excluded from the list of program expenses permitted. A [study](https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf) commissioned by the California Primary Care Assn. found that clinics could face up to $1.7 billion in collective penalties in the first year of the measure’s implementation.

**The basics**

[Proposition 45](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-45-ceqa-housing-data-center-voter-guide) would impose stricter deadlines on environmental reviews, permits and court challenges. Agencies would have to spell out application requirements up-front and could not make repeated requests for more information or project changes. The measure caps public comment periods, while current law only sets minimum lengths. It also limits what courts may consider in California Environmental Quality Act lawsuits.

### [Your guide to Proposition 45: Faster CEQA review for housing and infrastructure](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-45-ceqa-housing-data-center-voter-guide)

Prop 45 seeks to overhaul the law often blamed for delaying construction and driving up its cost: the California Environmental Quality Act.

 Oct. 1, 2026 

**The impact**

The law clearly would change the CEQA process; whether that would be for better or worse is the subject of debate. Backers say it would make the process faster and easier. Critics say it would roll back important environmental protections.

**Dig deeper**

The fight over Proposition 45 comes as California struggles to build enough housing to meet demand, causing prices to skyrocket. The price of housing, polls show, is a major issue for California voters.

But the proposition also is touching on another [hot-button issue: data centers](https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2026-10-14/californias-prop-45-aims-to-speed-construction-projects-opponents-say-data-centers-will-benefit). Supporters and foes are battling over whether the measure would make it easier to build more of those controversial facilities.

 **California Proposition 40**, the **One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative**, is on the [ballot](/California_2026_ballot_propositions "California 2026 ballot propositions") in [California](/California "California") as an [combined initiated constitutional amendment and state statute](/Combined_initiated_constitutional_amendment_and_state_statute "Combined initiated constitutional amendment and state statute") on [November 3, 2026](/California_2026_ballot_propositions "California 2026 ballot propositions").[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

A "**yes**" vote supports this initiative to levy a one-time 5% tax on the accumulated wealth of taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion, including shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest, to fund state health care programs, food assistance programs, and public education.

A "**no**" vote opposes this initiative to levy a one-time 5% tax on the accumulated wealth of taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion, including shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest, to fund state health care programs, food assistance programs, and public education.

  
 

[Competing ballot measures in 2026](/Superseding_initiative "Superseding initiative")

Two measures — [Proposition 41, the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative](/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 41, Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative (2026)") and [Proposition 42, the Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings Initiative](/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 42, Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings and Limit Retroactive Taxes Initiative (2026)") — are also on the November 3 ballot in California and contain competing measure provisions that would nullify Proposition 40 if all the measures are approved but Propositions 41 and 42 receive more votes than Proposition 40. Proposition 40 also contains a competing measure provision that would nullify Propositions 41 and 42 if Proposition 40 receives more votes.  
Read more about the conflict [here](#2026_competing_California_tax_measures).

## Overview

### What would the initiative do?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design) and [2026 competing California tax measures](#2026_competing_California_tax_measures)*

The initiative would enact a one-time tax of 5% on the accumulated wealth of taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion, including shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest. The tax would be retroactive and apply to taxpayers residing in the state as of January 1, 2026. The tax would be due with an individual's 2027 tax filings. The initiative would allow individuals to pay the tax in five equal installments beginning in 2027, with each subsequent payment subject to an annual deferral charge of 7.5% of the remaining unpaid balance.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

The initiative would create the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, where all taxes, interest, and penalties resulting from the initiative would be deposited. The fund would have two sub-accounts: the Billionaire Tax Health account, where 90% of the revenue would be deposited, and the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account with the remaining 10% of revenue. The initiative would fund Medi-Cal and other health coverage programs for low- and moderate-income individuals; health care access, benefits, and services; public education from K-14; and food assistance programs such as CalFresh, CalFAP, CalFood, or California's Universal Meals Program for school meals.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

Two measures — [Proposition 41, the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative](/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 41, Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative (2026)") and [Proposition 42, the Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings Initiative](/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 42, Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings and Limit Retroactive Taxes Initiative (2026)") — are also on the November 3 ballot in California and contain competing measure provisions that would nullify Proposition 40 if all the measures are approved but Propositions 41 and 42 receive more votes than Proposition 40. Proposition 40 also contains a competing measure provision that would nullify Propositions 41 and 42 if Proposition 40 receives more votes. 

### How would net worth be calculated?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design)*

To determine an individual's net worth, the initiative would account for the following assets:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   publicly traded securities at their market value on December 31, 2026;
*   private business interests;
*   assets under a sole proprietorship;
*   grantor trusts;
*   art, collectibles, intellectual property, vehicles, other financial instruments not publicly traded, and debts or liabilities owed to the individual ($5 million exclusion of total combined asset value from net worth);
*   Roth IRA or other Roth-type retirement accounts valued above $10 million;
*   property valued at more than $1 million transferred after October 15, 2025, for less than fair market value; and
*   dependent's assets in excess of $50,000.

Real estate and pensions would be excluded from the calculation of net worth.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

The initiative would account for the following debts as reductions to an individual's net worth:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   recourse debts for which the individual is personally liable;
*   nonrecourse debts up to the value of the collateral securing them; and
*   debts and other liabilities resulting from a sole proprietorship but not from a partnership, limited liability company, or other business entity.

### Have other states enacted similar taxes?

*See also: [Wealth tax ballot measures](#Wealth_tax_ballot_measures) and [Ballot measures related to income and wealth taxes, 2026](/Ballot_measures_related_to_income_and_wealth_taxes,_2026 "Ballot measures related to income and wealth taxes, 2026")*

The California wealth tax initiative would be the first ballot measure in the country to enact such a tax. In 2023, Texas voters approved [Proposition 3](/Texas_Proposition_3,_Prohibit_Taxes_on_Wealth_or_Net_Worth_Amendment_\(2023\) "Texas Proposition 3, Prohibit Taxes on Wealth or Net Worth Amendment (2023)") by a margin of 68% to 32%, amending the state constitution to prohibit the state legislature from enacting a wealth tax or net worth tax in the future. 

Additionally, in 2026, there are nine statewide ballot measures in six states related to income and wealth tax policy. Of these measures, two would allow, create, or increase income taxes; five would prohibit, cap, or decrease income taxes; one would allow, create, or increase wealth taxes; and one would prohibit, cap, or decrease wealth taxes. 

### Who supports and opposes the initiative?

*See also: [Support](#Support) and [Opposition](#Opposition)*

[Save California Health Care and Public Education](#Support), sponsored by [SEIU-UHW](/SEIU-UHW "SEIU-UHW"), is leading the Yes on 40 campaign in support of the initiative. U.S. Sen. [Bernie Sanders](/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") (D), U.S. Rep. [Ro Khanna](/Ro_Khanna "Ro Khanna") (D), [Democratic Party of California](/Democratic_Party_of_California "Democratic Party of California"), California Democratic Socialists of America, Teamsters California, and UNITE HERE Local 11 have endorsed Proposition 40. Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for SEIU-UHW, said, "We’re calling on California’s billionaires to step up and pay a one-time, emergency 5% tax to prevent the collapse of California healthcare and help fund California public K-14 education and state food assistance programs. This would protect healthcare jobs and ensure working people and families can get the care they need. The tax would be paid only by Californians worth more than $1 billion — which is a bit over 200 people who hold a combined wealth of $2 trillion."[\[2\]](#cite_note-support-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) 

[No on Prop 40](#Opposition) is leading the campaign in opposition to the initiative. U.S. Rep. [Kevin Kiley](/Kevin_Kiley "Kevin Kiley") (R), Gov. [Gavin Newsom](/Gavin_Newsom "Gavin Newsom") (D), gubernatorial candidates [Xavier Becerra](/Xavier_Becerra "Xavier Becerra") (D) and [Steve Hilton](/Steve_Hilton "Steve Hilton") (R), the [California Teachers Association](/California_Teachers_Association "California Teachers Association"), State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California oppose the initiative. Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said, "We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms. We make those decisions together through the elected Legislature, through a budget, and through the public process that voters built precisely to prevent any single interest from prevailing with disregard for the rest. At the same time, the fight to make the wealthiest Americans pay more in taxes is not one we should be fighting state by state. You may not be able to pick up and move to Texas or Florida to shelter your income from taxation, but I promise you that billionaires can, and do. Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes. The fight belongs at the federal level, where this broken system was created in the first place."[\[4\]](#cite_note-opposition-4)[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) 

As of October 22, 2026, the date the most recent campaign finance reports covered through, campaigns surrounding Proposition 40 reported $173.7 million in contributions, with two support committees reporting $33.2 million and five opposition committees reporting $140.5 million. Campaigns registered to support or oppose Proposition 40 conversely registered to support or oppose [Propositions 41](/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 41, Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative (2026)") and [42](/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 42, Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings and Limit Retroactive Taxes Initiative (2026)"). ## Measure design

*See also: [Text of measure](#Text_of_measure)*

**Click on the following sections** for summaries of the different provisions of the ballot measure. 

Expand All

Wealth tax on taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion

The initiative would levy a one-time tax of 5% on taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion, including shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest. A married couple would be considered one individual. The tax would be retroactive and apply to any taxpayer residing in the state as of January 1, 2026. For individuals with net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, the tax rate would be reduced by 0.1% (but not below 0%) for each $2 million their net worth falls below $1.1 billion. The tax would be due with an individual's 2027 tax filings.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

  
 

The initiative would allow individuals to pay the tax in five equal installments beginning in 2027, with each subsequent payment subject to an annual deferral charge of 7.5% of the remaining unpaid balance.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

Net worth calculation

To determine an individual's net worth, the initiative would account for the following assets:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

*   publicly traded securities at their market value on December 31, 2026;
*   private business interests;
*   assets under a sole proprietorship;
*   grantor trusts;
*   art, collectibles, intellectual property, vehicles, other financial instruments not publicly traded, and debts or liabilities owed to the individual ($5 million exclusion of total combined asset value from net worth);
*   Roth IRA or other Roth-type retirement accounts valued above $10 million;
*   property valued at more than $1 million transferred after October 15, 2025, for less than fair market value; and
*   dependent's assets in excess of $50,000.

Real estate and pensions would be excluded from the calculation of net worth.[\[7\]](#cite_note-lao-7) 

The initiative would account for the following debts as reductions to an individual's net worth:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   recourse debts for which the individual is personally liable;
*   nonrecourse debts up to the value of the collateral securing them; and
*   debts and other liabilities resulting from a sole proprietorship but not from a partnership, limited liability company, or other business entity.

The following debts or liabilities would not lower an individual's net worth:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   related-party debts;
*   charitable pledges made after October 15, 2025; and
*   contingent liabilities with outcomes uncertain within five years.

Revenue allocation

The initiative would create the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, where all taxes, interest, and penalties resulting from the initiative would be deposited. The fund would have two sub-accounts: the Billionaire Tax Health account, where 90% of the revenue would be deposited, and the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account with the remaining 10% of revenue. The initiative would require the health account to fund Medi-Cal and other health coverage programs for low- and moderate-income individuals, as well as health care access, benefits, and services. The initiative would require revenue in the education account to fund public education from K-14, reductions in federal or state appropriations, and reductions in food assistance programs such as CalFresh, CalFAP, CalFood, or California's Universal Meals Program for school meals.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

  
 

The initiative contains a provision that would exclude the revenue generated by the tax from the state’s General Fund when calculating the state minimum guarantee for education funding, which was enacted by [Proposition 98](/California_Proposition_98,_Mandatory_Education_Spending_Initiative_\(1988\) "California Proposition 98, Mandatory Education Spending Initiative (1988)") in 1988.

  
 

## Text of measure

### Ballot title

The ballot title is as follows: 

“ 

Imposes one-time tax on certain taxpayers. Initiative constitutional amendment and statute.[\[8\]](#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-8) 

” 

### Ballot summary

The ballot summary is as follows:[\[9\]](#cite_note-vg-9) 

“ 

Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit.[\[8\]](#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-8) 

” 

### Fiscal impact

The fiscal impact statement is as follows:[\[9\]](#cite_note-vg-9) 

“ 

Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. [\[8\]](#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-8) 

” 

### Petition summary

The summary provided for inclusion on signature petition sheets is as follows: 

“ 

Imposes one-time tax of up to 5% on taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion; covered assets include businesses, securities, art, collectibles, and intellectual property, but exclude real property and some pensions and retirement accounts. Allocates 90% of these tax revenues for health care, 10% for food assistance or education-related programs; prohibits using revenues to replace existing funding for these purposes. Exempts such tax revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding, budget reserves, and state spending limit. [\[8\]](#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-8)

### Constitutional changes

*See also: [Article XIII, California Constitution](/Article_XIII,_California_Constitution "Article XIII, California Constitution")*

The ballot measure would amend [Section 37 of Article XIII](/Article_XIII,_California_Constitution#Section_37 "Article XIII, California Constitution") of the [California Constitution](/California_Constitution "California Constitution"). The following underlined text would be added:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*Note*: Hover over the text and scroll to see the full text. 

Sec. 37. 

(a) This Section authorizes and enables a one-time tax on the accumulated wealth of California billionaires, imposed on those individuals who are California residents within the meaning of Sections 17014 and 17015.5 of the Revenue and Taxation Code as of the tax obligation date as defined in the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act. 

(b) The following definitions apply to this Section: 

(1) "Act" refers to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act. 

(2) "Reserve Fund" refers to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, created by this Act. 

(c) Notwithstanding any other provision of the Constitution, the Act provides for taxation on all forms of personal property and wealth, whether tangible or intangible, and allows for the classification of personal property and wealth for differential taxation or for exemption, for the purpose of imposing the one-time tax on the wealth of California billionaires. Personal property and wealth that is so taxed includes, but is not limited to, shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest therein. 

(d) The 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund is hereby created in the State Treasury. All revenues from the Act—including taxes, interest, and penalties, and less refunds—shall be deposited in the State Treasury by the State Controller to the credit of the Reserve Fund. After accounting for administrative expenses as provided by law, the Controller shall allocate and transfer the remaining moneys in the Reserve Fund to the following sub-accounts, which are hereby created: 90% to the Billionaire Tax Health Account and 10% to the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account. The moneys in the Billionaire Tax Health Account and the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account shall be allocated as provided by law. 

(e) Notwithstanding any other law, the Reserve Fund is a special fund, permanently separate and apart from the General Fund or any other state fund or account. The taxes and the moneys resulting from the Act shall not be considered to be part of the General Fund, as that term is used in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 16300) of Part 2 of Division 4 of Title 2 of the Government Code; and shall not be considered "General Fund revenues," "state revenues," "moneys," or "proceeds of taxes" under Section 8 of Article XIIIB for the purposes of any section of Article XIIIB, or Sections 8 or 8.5 of Article XVI. Any revenue raised through the Act shall also not be considered "personal income taxes paid on net capital gains" for purposes of Section 20 of Article XVI. The taxes levied by this Act are not "ad valorem taxes on real property" for purposes of Section 1 of Article XIIIA. To the extent any provision of Article XIIIA would otherwise be construed to limit, restrict, or apply to the rate, base, valuation, or imposition of the tax authorized by this Section, that provision shall not apply to, and is superseded by, this Section. Notwithstanding Section 16305.7 of the Government Code, any interest or dividends earned on moneys in the Reserve Fund shall be retained in the Reserve Fund and used solely for the specific purposes set forth in this subdivision and as provided by the Act. 

(f) "Appropriations subject to limitation" of each entity of government and the state under Article XIIIB shall not include appropriations of revenue from the Reserve Fund. No adjustment in the appropriations limit of any entity of government shall be required pursuant to Section 3 of Article XIIIB as a result of revenue being deposited in or appropriated from the Reserve Fund. 

(g) Except as provided in Sections 16310 and 16381 of the Government Code as those sections read on January 1, 2025, and except as otherwise provided in this Act, moneys in the Reserve Fund shall not be borrowed, loaned, or otherwise transferred to the General Fund or any other state or local fund or account. Moneys deposited into the Reserve Fund shall only be used for the specific purposes provided by law. Action shall not be taken that permanently or temporarily changes the status of the Reserve Fund or borrows, diverts, or appropriates the moneys in the Reserve Fund in a manner inconsistent with this subdivision. 

(h) Notwithstanding Section 32 or any other provision of law, a facial challenge to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act is authorized to be adjudicated through a validation action under Chapter 6 of Part 27 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, Section 50314 without requiring the payment of the tax claimed to be facially invalid. This subdivision is adopted without implication as to current authority or the development of law other than this Act. Nothing in this subdivision limits any taxpayer's right to pay a tax imposed under this Act and seek a refund or judicial review, or to bring any other action that is otherwise authorized by law and not inconsistent with this subdivision.[\[8\]](#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-8)

### Arguments

*   **Jack Guidi from Americans for Tax Reform:** "The tax is retroactive and would apply to all eligible residents beginning January 1st, 2026. However, the earliest this tax could go into effect would be November 2026. This means California could end up losing tax revenue even if the ballot initiative doesn’t pass, as it incentivizes wealthy residents to escape before the tax passes."[](https://atr.org/californias-billionaire-tax-is-a-policy-disaster/)
*   **Jon Hartley, a policy fellow at the Hoover Institution, and Arthur Laffer, president of Laffer Associates:** "California doesn’t suffer from too little taxation. Its top marginal state income-tax rate is 13.3%, the highest in the U.S. Capital-gains taxes, corporate taxes and sales taxes are all at or near the highest in the nation as well. The wealth-tax initiative would amplify the problem of revenue volatility by taxing volatile paper valuations while assuming the tax base will sit still when the bill arrives."[](https://www.wsj.com/opinion/california-wealth-tax-backers-ignore-proposition-13-lessons-e4e6d368?gaa_at=eafs&gaa_n=AWEtsqdW59R-KBu3FeOV4zyfedIdBLtRQddcmeai-6Le54_YRiG11y4UP9E0&gaa_ts=6976bc40&gaa_sig=x5-B6l3Ld5EI_ZmjgusNFIX-pbjv8FG0Bz7c-J5yZYCb8-1mh-LC6Xp5KFR4TBaZ1U_0g2wVSBwCZzOe4auk0Q%3D%3D)
*   **Aaron Withe, chief executive officer of the Freedom Foundation:** "SEIU and its enablers call this a healthcare funding measure — a response to federal Medicaid reforms. It isn’t. California already has the highest income tax rates in the nation. Its budget problems aren’t a revenue problem. They’re a spending problem that’s outpaced even California’s substantial tax base for years."[](https://www.realclearpolicy.com/articles/2026/05/08/californias_billionaire_tax_could_reach_far_beyond_billionaires_1181592.html)
*   **Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California President Jodi Hicks:** "The initiative’s uncertain impacts on the state budget and lack of specificity on health care allocations will do more harm than good in the long term."[](https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/06/05/wealth-tax-backlash-data-nerds-and-newsoms-regret-00951373?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=cc082b66-1195-4295-92b5-e72037c7247e)
*   **Gov. Gavin Newsom (D):** "We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms. We make those decisions together through the elected Legislature, through a budget, and through the public process that voters built precisely to prevent any single interest from prevailing with disregard for the rest. At the same time, the fight to make the wealthiest Americans pay more in taxes is not one we should be fighting state by state. You may not be able to pick up and move to Texas or Florida to shelter your income from taxation, but I promise you that billionaires can, and do. Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes. The fight belongs at the federal level, where this broken system was created in the first place."[](https://gavinnewsom.substack.com/p/its-time-for-a-national-billionaires)
